cards.title: Two Rules That Cost You Nothing
cards.content:
Almost every change in this book asks something of you. Buy this, cook that, walk after dinner, get under a bar twice a week. Those all pay, and they all cost.

This lesson is different. Both rules here are **free**. Nothing leaves your plate, nothing gets weighed, nothing gets banned. You keep the bread, the rice, the potatoes and the pudding.

**Rule one: eat in order.** Vegetables and protein before starch.

**Rule two: front-load the day.** A consistent ten to twelve hour eating window, weighted early.

That is the whole lesson. The rest is showing you exactly how to run them at a restaurant table, a canteen tray, a family dinner at eight, and a curry on a Friday night. And showing you honestly where they work less well, and who should not use rule two at all.

cards.title: Rule One: Vegetables And Protein First
cards.content:
Take any meal you already eat and split it into three groups. **Fibre** (salad, greens, slaw, soup, roasted veg). **Protein and fat** (fish, eggs, chicken, tofu, beans, cheese, olive oil, nuts). **Starch** (rice, bread, potato, pasta, oats).

Then eat them in that order: fibre, then protein and fat, then starch. Not as a rigid ritual with a stopwatch, just as a habit of the fork. Finish the salad before you start the chicken. Finish the chicken before you start the potatoes.

The same meal, eaten in that sequence, produces a **lower and flatter glucose rise** and a **smaller insulin response** than the identical meal eaten starch-first or all mixed together.

Read that again, because it is the strange part: **the food is identical**. The portion is identical. You did not swap the white rice for brown, you did not halve the chips, you did not skip the bread. You changed the sequence, and the body did the rest.

cards.title: What The Order Does Inside You
cards.content:
Three mechanisms, all of them ordinary physiology.

1. **Gastric emptying slows.** Fibre, protein and fat arriving first make the stomach hand food over to the small intestine more slowly. The starch that follows is released in a trickle rather than a flood.

2. **The rate of arrival falls.** Glucose appears in the bloodstream as fast as it is digested and absorbed. Same total sugar, spread over more minutes, means a lower peak. The area under the curve matters, but the **peak and the steepness** matter too, and those are what sequence changes most.

3. **The gut speaks first.** Protein and fat reaching the small intestine trigger **L-cells** to release **GLP-1**, the incretin hormone that boosts glucose-dependent insulin release and slows gastric emptying further. Eating the starch last means it arrives into a gut that is already primed and already braking.

None of this is exotic. It is the same machinery a GLP-1 drug leans on, nudged gently by the order of your fork.

cards.title: The Evidence, Honestly
cards.content:
The clearest work on meal order comes from **Alpana Shukla** and colleagues at **Weill Cornell Medicine**. Their studies are small crossover trials, typically fifteen to twenty people, mostly with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, each person eating the same meal in different sequences on different days and having their blood sampled for a few hours afterwards.

What they found, repeatedly: eating vegetables and protein before the carbohydrate produced **markedly lower post-meal glucose**, **lower insulin**, and a **higher GLP-1 response** than the same meal eaten carbohydrate-first.

Now the honest part. These are small studies over a few hours. There is no long trial showing that meal order alone changes heart attacks or HbA1c a decade later. The size of the effect varies between people, and it shrinks when the meal is genuinely mixed.

So hold it correctly: **the direction of effect is consistent and the mechanism is well understood, the magnitude is uncertain, and the cost is zero.** A free intervention with a plausible mechanism and consistent short-term data does not need a twenty-year outcome trial before you try it tonight.

cards.title: The Restaurant Meal
cards.content:
You are out for dinner. The bread basket lands before you have taken your coat off. Here is the whole play.

1. **Order a side salad or a soup with the starters.** Not instead of anything. As well. This is the only addition you make.

2. **Ask for it to come before the bread**, or ask them to hold the bread until the salad arrives. Waiters do this a hundred times a night and will not blink.

3. **Eat the salad. Then the protein.** Steak, sea bass, chicken, halloumi, dahl, whatever you ordered.

4. **Bread and chips last.** Same bread. Same chips. Later in the meal.

5. **Walk ten to fifteen minutes afterwards.** Park further away, walk to the station, take the long way home.

What you did not do: read the menu for the healthy options, order a salad instead of the thing you wanted, or announce a diet to the table. You added one side and rearranged your own fork.

cards.title: The Canteen Tray And The Home Dinner
cards.content:
**The work canteen tray.** Take the salad even when it looks like an afterthought under a heat lamp. Put it on the tray first so it is the thing nearest your hand. Sit down, eat the salad, then the main protein, then the rice or the chips. The tray held exactly the same food it always did. You reordered the tray.

If the salad bar is genuinely inedible, a pot of soup, a piece of fruit eaten first, or a small tub of olives does most of the same job.

**The home dinner.** This one is easier because you control the table. Say the meal is **salmon, greens and buttered new potatoes**.

1. **Put the greens on the table first**, dressed with olive oil and lemon, and eat them while the rest rests.

2. **Then the salmon.**

3. **Serve the potatoes in a bowl in the middle** and pass them round at the end, rather than plating everything at once.

That single serving change, a bowl in the middle instead of a full plate, is what makes rule one automatic at home.

cards.question: Pub dinner: garlic bread, a chicken thigh, a green salad and roast potatoes are all coming. Which sequence follows rule one?

options.text: Garlic bread while you wait, then the salad, then the chicken and potatoes
Green salad first, then the chicken, then the potatoes and garlic bread
Cancel the garlic bread and the potatoes and eat only the salad and chicken
Eat everything together as it arrives, but leave half the potatoes

cards.explanation: Fibre, then protein and fat, then starch. The tempting wrong answer is cancelling the bread and potatoes, because it feels more virtuous, but that is a different intervention entirely: it is subtraction, it costs you something, and it is the kind of thing people abandon. Rule one is free precisely because nothing leaves the table. Bread while you wait is the common default and the worst option here, since it puts the fastest starch into an empty stomach.

cards.title: When You Cannot Separate The Meal
cards.content:
Some meals refuse to be sorted. A sandwich is bread and filling in one bite. A curry is sauce over rice. A stew has potatoes in it. Be honest about this: **in a fully mixed meal the effect is smaller**, because you cannot control what arrives first. But partial separation still beats none.

**The sandwich lunch.** Add a side salad, a pot of soup, or a small tub of olives and cherry tomatoes. Eat that first, all of it, then the sandwich. If you can, eat the sandwich open-faced with the filling first, but do not turn lunch into a performance. The side eaten first is ninety per cent of the available benefit.

**Curry with rice.** Serve the rice in a separate bowl, not underneath. Start with the salad or raita and any vegetable side, then the curry itself with a fork, then bring the rice in. If it is a takeaway, order a vegetable side dish alongside and eat that first while the rest is being plated up.

**Stew or one-pot.** Spoon out the vegetables and meat first, leave the potatoes and the bread until the end.

When genuine separation is impossible, do the next best thing: **a proper vegetable or protein starter before the mixed dish arrives.**

cards.title: Tonight: Change Only The Order
cards.content:
One meal. One variable. Do not improve the food, do not shrink the portion, do not add a walk yet. Cook exactly what you were going to cook.

1. **Plate the vegetables separately** and eat them on their own, all of them, before you touch anything else.

2. **Then the protein**, on its own.

3. **Then the starch**, the same portion you always have.

Then notice two things, and only two.

• **At ninety minutes**: is your energy sharp, flat, or heavy? One word.

• **At three hours**: is your hunger urgent, present, or calm? One word.

Two words in your phone. That is the entire log. If any kind of food logging raises anxiety for you, skip the log completely and keep the order. The plate is the intervention, not the record of it.

One meal will not tell you much. That is fine. You are not measuring a result tonight, you are proving to yourself that the change is genuinely free.

cards.title: Rule Two: Front-Load The Day
cards.content:
Your ability to handle a meal is not constant. **Insulin sensitivity is highest in the morning** and falls as the day goes on, and the **beta cells** that release insulin follow their own circadian rhythm too. Carefully controlled laboratory studies, including forced desynchrony experiments where researchers uncouple people from the clock on the wall, show the same identical meal producing a **larger and longer glucose rise in the biological evening** than in the biological morning.

There is a hormonal handle on this. **Melatonin** rises in the evening, and the beta cell carries melatonin receptors. Melatonin damps insulin secretion, which is sensible when you are supposed to be asleep and unhelpful when you are eating a bowl of pasta at half past ten.

The practical version is not dramatic. **A consistent ten to twelve hour eating window, weighted early.** Something like seven-thirty in the morning to six or seven in the evening. Breakfast and lunch carry more of the day's food than dinner does.

And note the word **consistent**. A steady window you keep most days beats a heroic window you keep twice.

cards.title: The Same Bowl At 8am And At 9pm
cards.content:
Picture one bowl of pasta. Same weight, same sauce, same person. Eaten at eight in the morning it produces a moderate rise that comes back down fairly promptly. Eaten at nine at night, the identical bowl produces a **higher peak that stays elevated for longer**.

Nothing about the pasta changed. The body receiving it did. Insulin sensitivity has fallen, beta cell responsiveness has fallen, and melatonin has begun to rise.

There is also a small trial worth knowing about. **Courtney Peterson** and colleagues ran a five-week crossover study of **early time-restricted eating** in a small group of men with prediabetes. Eating the same food within an early window improved insulin sensitivity, beta cell responsiveness and blood pressure, **even though body weight was deliberately held constant**. Eight participants, so treat it as a signal rather than proof, but it points the same way as the mechanism does.

The useful conclusion is modest: **when you eat is a lever, and it is a free one.**

cards.question: Three people each eat within a ten-hour window. Which pattern best matches rule two?

options.text: 11am to 9pm, because skipping breakfast makes the overnight fast longest
All three are equivalent, because the window is ten hours in every case
7am to 5pm, because the same window sits earlier in the day
2pm to midnight, because it fits around evening social life most easily

cards.explanation: Length is not the only variable; placement is. The identical window sitting earlier lines up with the hours when insulin sensitivity and beta cell responsiveness are highest. The tempting wrong answer is that all three are equivalent, since they are all ten hours, but that ignores the circadian half of the mechanism. One caveat: a 7am to 5pm window is impractical for many lives. The principle is an earlier centre of gravity you can actually keep, not a specific pair of clock times.

cards.title: Three Real Schedules
cards.content:
The ten to twelve hour window is a default, not a decree. Here is how it survives contact with an actual life.

**The late-finishing shift.** You get home at nine and you are genuinely hungry. Do not eat a full second dinner at half past nine because you skipped one at six. Move the main meal to your break at work, six-ish, and have something small and protein-led when you get in: a bowl of Greek yoghurt with berries and nuts, or two boiled eggs with tomatoes. The window ends up wide on those days. That is fine.

**The 8pm family dinner.** Keep it. Dinner with people you love is not a variable to optimise away. Instead move breakfast and lunch a little earlier, make **lunch the biggest meal of the day**, and let the eight o'clock dinner be the smallest plate rather than the largest.

**The night out.** Eat late, enjoy it properly, walk home if you can. The next day you return to the normal window. No compensating, no skipping breakfast to make up for it, no penance.

The target is a **slightly earlier centre of gravity, kept most days**, not a rigid window kept perfectly.

cards.title: Safety: Who Should Not Narrow The Window
cards.content:
Rule two is not for everyone, and this matters more than the physiology.

**Do not use a restricted eating window if you are:**

• **Pregnant or breastfeeding.** Nutrient and energy needs are elevated and continuous. This is not the time.

• **Living with any history of disordered eating.** Rules about when you may and may not eat are a well-known trigger. The plate stays; the window goes.

• **Underweight, or losing weight you did not intend to lose.** Speak to a clinician about the weight loss first.

• **A child or an adolescent.** Growth is the priority, full stop.

• **Taking insulin or a sulfonylurea** (gliclazide, glimepiride, glipizide) **without medical supervision.** Narrowing the window while also eating in order and walking after meals lowers glucose from several directions at once. On these medicines that can cause **hypoglycaemia**, and it needs a dose conversation with your doctor or diabetes nurse before you start, not after.

• **On any medication that must be taken with food** at fixed times.

One reassurance: **rule one has no timing requirement at all.** Eating in order is safe for everybody on this list. If rule two is not for you, run rule one and skip the rest of this lesson without losing anything important.

cards.title: Set Your Window This Week
cards.content:
Assuming the safety card cleared you, this takes about two minutes to set up.

1. **Pick your first bite time.** Not an aspiration, the time you actually eat on a normal Tuesday. Most people land between seven and eight in the morning.

2. **Add eleven hours. That is your kitchen close.** First bite at 7:30am gives a close of 6:30pm. Aim to finish before it, not exactly on it.

3. **Make lunch the biggest meal.** Front-loading is about the weight of food as much as the clock. If dinner ends up the smallest plate of the day, you have done the harder half of rule two.

4. **Water, black coffee and plain tea outside the window are fine.** No milk-based coffees, no snacks, no juice.

And the part that decides whether this lasts: **two days a week will not match.** A birthday, a late train, a work dinner. When that happens you do not restart the plan, you do not compensate the next day, you simply return to the window at the next meal.

A twelve-hour window kept five days a week beats a ten-hour window kept twice and then abandoned. **Shorter is not automatically better** — trials of eight-hour windows have not reliably outperformed simply eating three normal meals a day.

cards.title: The Marker You Can Actually Feel
cards.content:
Here is a thing the internet will not tell you honestly. If your pancreas works normally, **you cannot feel a single meal's glucose curve.** There is no sensation attached to going from 6 to 8 millimoles per litre and back. People who report feeling their glucose after one sandwich are, with the best will in the world, mostly reporting expectation.

So do not judge these two rules meal by meal. You have no instrument, and the honest answer to "did that work?" after one dinner is that you cannot know.

What you can notice is the **downstream** effect, and it takes several days.

• **Afternoon energy.** The three o'clock trough that arrives after a starch-forward lunch tends to soften once lunch is eaten in order and the day is weighted earlier.

• **Evening hunger.** Less of the nine o'clock foraging that follows a big, late, fast-rising meal.

• **Sleep and morning appetite.** Often steadier when the last meal is not sitting on top of bedtime.

Give it four or five days before you form an opinion, and judge **the pattern of your afternoons**, not the feeling after any single meal.

cards.title: The Seven Day Card
cards.content:
One card, two rows, seven days. Put it on the fridge or make it two lines in your notes app.

**Row one — did I eat in order at my main meal?** Not every meal. One meal a day, the biggest one. Tick or leave blank.

**Row two — did I finish eating before my kitchen close?** Same deal. Tick or leave blank.

How to read it at the end of the week:

• **Five of seven on both rows is a good week.** That is the target.

• **Seven of seven is not the target.** If you are hitting it perfectly you are probably either lucky with your schedule or being rigid about it, and rigidity is the thing that ends plans.

• **Two or fewer on either row** means the setup is wrong, not that you are. Move the kitchen close later, or pick a different main meal to apply rule one to.

And the standing rule: **if ticking boxes makes you anxious, throw the card away and keep the plate.** The order and the timing are the intervention. The card is only scaffolding, and scaffolding comes down.

cards.question: You have run both rules for five days. You do not have diabetes and you have no glucose sensor. What is the honest marker to judge them by?

options.text: How full you feel in the twenty minutes after each meal
Whether you can feel your glucose falling an hour after eating
The number on the scale each morning
Your afternoon energy across several days, and whether the 3pm slump softened

cards.explanation: With a normally working pancreas you cannot perceive a single meal's glucose curve, so any felt sense of it is mostly expectation. Fullness is confounded by volume and fibre, and morning scale weight moves with water, salt and gut contents over days like these. The downstream, multi-day marker is the usable one: a softer afternoon trough and less late-evening foraging. Judge the pattern of a week, never the feeling after one dinner.

<rect x="0" y="0" width="1100" height="1100" fill="#1a1a2e"/>
<text x="550" y="70" text-anchor="middle" fill="#ffd700" font-weight="bold" font-size="36">THE 3PM TEST</text>
<text x="550" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="#888" font-size="24">What should you actually watch?</text>
<text x="610" y="248" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f59e0b" font-size="22">The hour that tells the truth</text>
<line x1="120" y1="330" x2="980" y2="330" stroke="#888" stroke-width="3"/>
<circle cx="610" cy="330" r="46" fill="rgba(245,158,11,0.12)" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="3"/>
<circle cx="150" cy="330" r="12" fill="#6366f1"/>
<circle cx="380" cy="330" r="12" fill="#6366f1"/>
<circle cx="610" cy="330" r="12" fill="#f59e0b"/>
<circle cx="840" cy="330" r="12" fill="#6366f1"/>
<text x="150" y="400" text-anchor="middle" fill="#888" font-size="18">7am</text>
<text x="380" y="400" text-anchor="middle" fill="#888" font-size="18">11am</text>
<text x="610" y="400" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f59e0b" font-size="18">3pm</text>
<text x="840" y="400" text-anchor="middle" fill="#888" font-size="18">7pm</text>
<rect x="100" y="460" width="900" height="350" rx="20" fill="rgba(99,102,241,0.12)" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="550" y="518" text-anchor="middle" fill="#ffd700" font-size="24" font-weight="bold">YOU HAVE NO SENSOR</text>
<text x="550" y="578" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-size="20">You cannot feel one meal's glucose curve</text>
<text x="550" y="616" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-size="20">if your pancreas is working normally.</text>
<text x="550" y="670" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-size="20">So do not look for it. Look at what the</text>
<text x="550" y="708" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-size="20">curve produces two hours later.</text>
<text x="550" y="768" text-anchor="middle" fill="#ffd700" font-size="22">Afternoon energy, several days running.</text>
<rect x="120" y="880" width="860" height="100" rx="20" fill="rgba(255,215,0,0.1)" stroke="#ffd700" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="550" y="942" text-anchor="middle" fill="#ffd700" font-size="22">Judge the pattern, not the meal.</text>
</svg>
